children.text: Egypt tires you out if walked unguarded. Understand the main tourist routes, distinguish regional differences, and move with basic care — the trip itself isn't a dangerous country.
What matters isn't a one-word answer to "is Egypt safe." A trip from a
Cairo
hotel to the
Giza
pyramids, a
Luxor
trip touring tombs from morning, a Red Sea resort stay, and a trip toward North Sinai or border zones are completely different judgments inside the same country.

Most actual traveller problems aren't violent crime. Persistent touts, price negotiation, road roughness, heat, water and food care, places you can't photograph, and stares or calls toward women travelling alone. Don't treat lightly; most are handleable with prior knowledge.
First, think with the map
Egypt's safety needs splitting by region.
Cairo, Giza, Luxor,
Aswan
Abu Simbel
Alexandria
, Sharm el-Sheikh,
Hurghada
, and
Marsa Alam

are usual tourist places with daily traveller movement. Around major sites and hotels, police and tourist police presence is visible; at airports, museums, temples, and parts of roads, checkpoints and luggage checks occur.

North Sinai, Libyan border, areas near Sudan border, and military-controlled desert zones are separate from usual tourist judgment. Japan's MOFA, UK FCDO, US State Department, and Australia's Smartraveller all issue strong cautions on North Sinai, border zones, and parts of the desert. This doesn't mean Cairo and Luxor are at the same risk. Rather, in Egypt, separating "places you can go" from "places not for personal judgment" is the basis of safety.

Siwa, Bahariya, the White Desert, and Fayoum reserves are appealing desert destinations. Unlike city sightseeing, vehicle, permits, checkpoints, signal, and weather preparation matter. Don't enter remote desert without trusted local arrangement.
What most travellers actually meet
The most-told unpleasant Egypt experience is less crime than friction.

Around the Giza pyramids, calls about camels, carriages, photos, guidance, and souvenirs multiply. Things said "free" not being free, a short ride turning into a high bill, a person who looked like an official being unrelated — not rare.

The response isn't complex. Don't accept what you didn't ask for. Don't board camels or horses without setting price and time. Confirm entrance and ticket talk only at official windows. If unneeded, don't stop — say "la, shukran" briefly. Start explaining and the conversation continues.

In Cairo markets, the metro, stations, and crowded sites, pickpocketing and bag theft also need care. Leave the passport original in the hotel safe except when needed for transfer; carry copies or phone photos. Don't keep cash in one place. Don't walk with phone in the street-side hand. Not Egypt-specific — the basics of travelling a large tourist city.
Transfer safety
A risk easily missed in Egypt is the road.

Cairo traffic is hard to read on first arrival. Lanes, gaps between cars, crossings, and horn use differ from Japanese or European sense. Driving yourself on a short trip has little point. In cities, hotel-arranged cars, trusted drivers, and ride-hailing apps like Uber or Careem are realistic.

For long distance, domestic flights, trains, and private cars by itinerary. From Cairo to Luxor or Aswan, save time with a flight, enjoy as travel with a train. Road movement toward the Red Sea is common; in some cases, avoid long-distance night driving. On desert roads, rest stops, checkpoints, vehicle state, and driver experience tie directly to safety.
Cairo metro is practical, with women-only cars. For first-timers it can feel tense; for central movement, a useful way to avoid road traffic.
Health, water, heat
The most realistic Egypt-travel health risks are water, food, and heat.

Don't drink tap water. Use bottled water even for brushing teeth where possible. Raw vegetables, washed salads, and unpeeled fruit shift risk by shop or hotel water management. Foods served hot, fast-turning places, busy places with little holding — safer.

CDC suggests Egypt-bound travellers consider hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and typhoid vaccinations. From Japan too, consult a travel clinic or doctor before departure, matching your age, conditions, stay length, and destinations.

The heat in Luxor, Aswan, and Abu Simbel is a factor that shifts the itinerary. In summer sightseeing, moving in early morning and avoiding around noon is safety care. Hat, sunscreen, oral rehydration, and enough water are not comfort — they are health management.

For medical care, Cairo has private hospitals used by foreign travellers. Red Sea resorts, Luxor, and Aswan have facilities; specialisation and equipment vary. For serious illness or accident, evacuation may be needed; always include medical evacuation in travel insurance.
Women travellers and families
Egypt isn't a country where women can't travel alone. Not an easy country to walk either.

Women travelling alone should prepare for stares, calls, photo requests, and pushy conversation invitations. Mostly words and attitude; cumulative, they tire. In streets, base on covering shoulders and knees; in mosques, carry a hair-cover scarf. Use ride-hailing or hotel cars for late movement. Use women-only metro cars. With unease, leave the place. Just these change a lot.
At resorts, don't fully drop guard. Hotel and tour environments are comfortable; don't be alone with strangers, don't leave drinks unattended, don't leave children only to hotel or excursion staff.

For families, Egypt receives warmly. Children get called to often, with help when stuck. Sites aren't stroller-friendly. With sand, steps, narrow tomb passages, and few handrails, small children need carriers or close adult watching. Car child seats aren't standard; arrange in advance if needed.
Photos, drones, law
In Egypt, the difference between OK and not-OK photos matters.

Sites, streetscapes, food, the Nile, desert landscape are usually fine. Don't photograph military, police, checkpoints, military facilities, government facilities, bridges, canals, airports, security-related buildings.
Suez
Canal and bridge photos can be treated more strictly than traveller sense. When unsure, don't photograph.
Drones aren't to be casually brought and flown by travellers. Unauthorised entry or use leads to confiscation or trouble. For film or news purposes, confirm formal authorisation before travel.

Penalties for illegal drugs are very heavy; even small amounts produce serious results. Public intoxication, political statements, and critical posts about the government or security agencies aren't to be taken lightly by travellers. While in Egypt, awareness of being inside the country's law and social sense is needed.

For LGBTQ+ travellers, don't judge only on whether laws explicitly ban same-sex relations. Public-morality laws have been used, with large risk to public expression. Same-sex and opposite-sex couples alike — restraint with public intimacy is realistic.
Red Sea and water safety
In Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh, and Marsa Alam, the sea is the trip's centre. Safety here is water judgment more than security.

For snorkelling and diving, use licensed and reputable operators. Sea conditions, wind, current, boat safety management, guide ratios, and oxygen-equipment presence aren't visible by price alone. Even swimmers shouldn't overestimate experience at offshore reefs, open water, or current-prone sites.
Don't stand on coral, don't touch marine life, don't disrupt buoyancy for a photo. Environmental protection and your safety. When beaches close or swimming is forbidden, follow rather than ask why.
Emergency numbers
Numbers to remember in Egypt:
Police: 122
Ambulance: 123
Fire: 180
Tourist police: 126

For theft, scams, sightseeing trouble, and serious dispute with persistent touts, tourist police are the first consultation. Tourist-police presence exists at major sites. Phone-response language and speed vary; asking hotel, guide, and cruise staff for help simultaneously is realistic.
Japanese travellers — save the Japan embassy in Egypt's contact before departure. Passport loss, arrest, accident, hospitalisation — these don't close with tour operator or hotel alone.
A mindset for travelling Egypt safely
Egypt isn't a place to travel staying tense. Not a place to fully drop guard either.

A good itinerary is safety measure itself. Don't push on the first Cairo day. At Giza, set entrance, ticket, car, and guide in advance. In Luxor, avoid hot hours. Desert as arranged trip. On the Red Sea, don't choose a boat only on price. For night movement, split where to walk and where to take a car.
What's needed in Egypt isn't fear but reading. Read the place. Read the time. Read approach. Read your own tiredness.
Do that and Egypt isn't an excessively difficult country. The pyramids,
Valley of the Kings
, Aswan's Nile, Red Sea reefs, and White Desert mornings repay care.
Prepare well.
Then, prepared, leave for the trip easy.

deck: For Cairo, Giza, Luxor, Aswan, and Red Sea travellers — Egypt safety set out realistically by region, transfer, health, scams, and women travelling alone.
